h1: Keeping licence documents ready for a surprise inspection
title: Licence Papers for a Surprise Inspection | Craft Beer School
desc: How to keep brewery licence documents, registers and stock records ready so a surprise excise or food inspection takes an hour, not a day.
teaser: Inspectors rarely phone ahead. The breweries that relax when they walk in are the ones whose files were ready last month too.
standfirst: Excise, food safety, fire and pollution officials can all visit an Indian brewery without warning. What they check is mostly paper and numbers. If those are tidy and current, the visit is short. If not, a small gap becomes a notice.
sections: What an inspector actually looks at

Most surprise visits follow the same pattern. The officer checks that your licences are valid and on display, then reads your registers against what is physically in the tanks and the cold room. The questions are simple. Is this licence current? Does this register match these tanks? Who signed this entry?

For a brewery, the excise side carries most of the weight: brewing records, fermentation and storage registers, daily stock and sales. They also want any wastage or dumped beer accounted for. Food safety officials look at your FSSAI licence, water test reports, medical fitness certificates for food handlers and temperature logs.
Keep one master file, not a drawer

Build a single licence file, physical and scanned, with one section per approval:

  • Excise licence and its latest renewal receipt.
  • FSSAI licence or registration.
  • Fire NOC and the last fire equipment service record.
  • Pollution control board consent.
  • Trade or shop licence and signage permission.
  • Groundwater NOC, if you run a borewell.
  • Lift and boiler certificates, where they apply.

On the first page, keep a one sheet summary: licence, number, issuing office, expiry date and the person responsible. Review it on the first working day of every month. Anything expiring within 90 days gets flagged in red.

An excise officer can dip a tank or read its gauge, then compare that with your register. The numbers have to agree within the tolerance your state allows. If a 1,000 litre fermenter is recorded at 960 litres and the sight glass shows 900, you need an explanation, ideally written down before anyone asks.

Write registers daily, not at the end of the week. Record losses as they happen: trub and yeast at transfer, beer lost to a burst hose, a batch dumped for infection. A dumped batch with no paperwork looks like undeclared sales. A dumped batch with a dated note, the reason and a witness signature looks like a brewery having a bad day.

Many licences must be displayed at the premises, usually near the entrance or the counter. Officers notice a missing frame before anything else. Keep originals safe and display certified copies where your state allows it.

Display your licence hours and the legal drinking age, which differs by state, where staff and guests can see them. A taproom manager who knows where every display sits and can open the master file in two minutes, sets the tone of the whole visit.

The founder who handles all the licensing is often travelling when the officer arrives. Name two people who can greet an inspector, offer a seat, find the file and call the right person. Give them a short script: be polite, cooperate, ask for the officer's name and office, take notes on what was checked, never argue on the floor.

If an officer raises an issue, ask for it in writing and agree a date to respond. Then call your licensing consultant the same day. Questions answered on paper in a week go better than promises made on the spot.

Paper gets damp, lost or borrowed. Keep a scanned copy of every licence, renewal receipt and certificate in a shared folder that the founder, manager and head brewer can open on a phone. Name files the same way every time: licence name, number and expiry date. When a licence is renewed, file the new copy and move the old one to an archive folder rather than deleting it.

Do the same with registers where your state allows digital records alongside the paper ones. A photograph of each day's register page, taken at closing, gives you a backup if a page is damaged. It also shows you quickly when someone has stopped filling it in.

Some brewers go further and keep production records in a spreadsheet that mirrors the excise register: batch number, volume at each transfer, losses and sales. Reconciling that sheet against the register every Monday takes 20 minutes. It catches the gap long before an officer does, which is the whole point of the exercise.
Run your own inspection every quarter

Once a quarter, pick a day without warning and run a mock inspection. One person plays the officer. Check expiries, compare two tanks with the register, open the temperature logs and ask a new bartender where the fire extinguishers are. Note every gap and fix it within a week.

Compliance sits alongside costing, staffing and sales as one of the routines that keep a brewery open. Building those routines so they run without the founder in the room takes more than a checklist. Our guide to annual licence renewals covers the calendar side.

Your first step: print the one page licence summary today and fill in every expiry date you can find.
faqs: Which inspections can happen without notice at a brewery?
Excise, food safety, fire and pollution officials can all visit. Excise usually checks registers against tank volumes, while food safety checks licences, water reports and hygiene.
How often should brewery registers be updated?
Daily. Registers written at the end of the week rarely match the tanks. Losses recorded late look suspicious.
What should staff do if an inspector arrives and the owner is away?
Greet the officer, cooperate, open the master licence file and call the named responsible person. Note what was checked and ask for any issue in writing.
